I have the plans and specifications here with reference to these buildings. The tenders received were as follows:-M. Sullivan, Kingston, $77,930; Doran & Devlin, Ottawa, $78,500; McKelvey & Birch, Kingston, $83,000; Elliott Bros., Kingston, $85,000. The department accepted the tender of Mr. Sullivan which was the lowest.
What was the tender of Elliott Brothers?
Are these the residences for the men which have cost over $100,000?
Yes, my hon. friend can look at the plans.

I don't want to look at the plans for I have seen the buildings themselves, and I think it would be a good thing for the country if the Minister of Public Works took a look at these buildings himself, for I believe he would come to the conclusion that not more than one-half of the money should have been expended. I know from repeated visits to Kingston that some buildings were required there, but to spend such a sum for sixteen little residences is altogether out of proportion to the value obtained. I saw them on Sunday afternoon, and while they are substantially built two story houses, no one would ever suppose they could have cost anything like $100,000. When I heard on Monday of the enormous cost of these buildings I was as astonished as I have been at anything this government has yet done. A dozen residences were required for non-commissioned officers, &c. If you got value for the $100,000 I would not find any fault, but when people are paying a price of $6,000 or $7,000 for a building they ought to have the equivalent of a building worth more than $3,000.	*
Did the tenders of McKelvey & Birch or Elliott Brothers, of Kingston, include anything more than the building, the plumbing or fixings?

Nothing but the construction of the buildings, it was the same with all the contractors' tenders. I am glad my hon. friend admits the necessity for these buildings, that of course puts us forward a considerable distance. As to the cost, I do not know that we could have gone about any better way of getting the buildings constructed as cheaply as possible. We advertised for tenders quite widely, inviting the attention of contractors and received tenders from four different contractors, ranging from $77,000 up to $85,000. We accepted the lowest tender. We might have been severely criti-Mr. PUGSLEY.
cised if we had made a private contract with any one of these firms to erect the building, but we went about it in the usual approved way and having received tenders that in the opinion of the chief architect were reasonable, we awarded the contract.

The contract given to Sullivan was for $77,739, for a building which is to cost $112,000, the extra cost being to cover the putting in of the heating, &c. Was any of this $34,000 extra done by tender?

Tenders were called for
the electric lighting and wiring. The work of heating was given to the contractor at a figure he furnished which the chief architect certified to be fair and reasonable.

The minister said he would be open to censure if the work had not been given by tender, but according to his own statement a considerable part of it was not given by tender. I take the view that the tender of $77,COO was for a complete building. Sullivan, who had the contract for putting up the building, is a contractor. McKelvey & Birch and Elliott Brothers are hardware merchants and plumbers, and I am a little surprised that these men should put in tenders for this work if their tenders did not cover something along the line of their own business. I am also surprised at the cost of this building. I visited it last Saturday and was more astonished than ever. I would ask the attention of the minister to the cost of some of the prominent buildings in Kingston. The old Queen's Arts buildings, erected 30 years ago, cost $50,000. The new Arts building cost $60,000; Grant Hall, $45,000; Ontario Hall, $80,000, Fleming Hall, $50,000; new Medical Hall, $50,000. Here we have 16 cottages costing $112,000 to accommodate the civil subordinate staff. At P-61 of the Auditor General's Report it is said they are for servants' quarters. Either the Auditor General is wrong or the minister is wrong in his answer to me. I want to enter a protest against this reckless waste of public money. This is not the only instance we have had of reckless waste of money In the neighbourhood of Kingston for military purposes. You are asking $15,000 for stables and $15,000 for a veterinary college. You erected some three years ago a stable at the entrance to the Military College grounds and there has not been a horse inside that stable; it is standing there and the hinges are rusting on the doors. I think this extravagance should be condemned for it cannot be called anything else than reckless extravagance.

The difference between the cost and value of these buildings is very striking. Has not the minister on his staff some official who makes an approximate estimate of the cost of a building when he calls for tenders? It is no use to say the

contract is given to the lowest tenderer, as there may be collusion between tenderers.
I presume the department is not bound to accept the lowest tender, and somebody in the department should be responsible for the cost of the building.

My hon. friend may rest assured that in the Public Works Department, which has ibeen established since confederation, we have men who do know the value of buildings. The chief architect has been there for 30 odd years under the various governments we have had during that time. He is a man in whose judgment I and my predecessors have had every confidence, and until I have something more than the opinion of gentlemen who, I suppose, have not been through these buildings and know nothing about the interior work and details, I shall continue to hold my faith in the judgment of the chief architect.
Did your architect estimate on the cost of this building?
Yes, Mr. Ewart estimated the cost to be $96,000. That was before the contract was let.
Is that for the building complete?
Yes.
Has the minister an itemized estimate there of material, &c., required?

No, I have not the items of Mr. Ewart's estimate, but I have no objection to bringing it down. My hon. friends sought to draw a comparison between this and certain buildings in Kingston, but you cannot compare one building with another unless you know something about the interior of the buildings, how many partition walls there may be, the number of bathrooms, heating apparatus, plumbing, &c. In some cases the chief architect thinks the lowest tender is too high and new tenders are called for, but in this case he considered that the amount for the building was reasonable and recommended that the contract should be given to the lowest tenderer.

It appears that the cost of each one of these dwellings to the government will be $7,000 for a two-story building with only the end walls, so to speak, practically all one building. An ordinary man erecting such a building could not find any way of spending that much money in it.

For the information of the Minister of Public Works, the buildings to which I referred were all in connection with Queen's University at Kingston, and as they are divided into a great many classrooms, &c., they are not an inexpensive type of structure. These dwellings, which cost $7,000 each, contain upstairs, two bed-484
rooms and one bath-room, and down stairs a kitchen, living room, hall and vestibule. If you divide the number of rooms into the cost you will see that each room costs $1,500 or $1,600. The whole thing is indefensible and absolutely ridiculous. It is an evidence of the most reckless extravagance ever indulged in by any government in any civilized country.

I am not here to try to obstruct public buildings because I believe that public buildings should be constructed and we are here for that purpose; we are here to construct public buildings wherever we can. But it is our duty to see that the moneys of the country are judiciously and well spent. We have the statement made by the Minister of Public Works that the contract for these buildings, which were estimated by the architect to cost $96,000, are now costing us, under present methods, $112,000, or 16 per cent over the estimate. I am interested somewhat in real estate and I know something about the construction of ordinary small buildings such as these, and I say that $3,000 each would be a high price for these buildings. Reference has been made to the_ subject of advertising for tenders. The minister has stated that in this case the department advertised very widely, and perhaps they did, but while he said the other day that he had decided to abolish the patronage system, he said at the same time that he was going to continue to advertise in the Liberal papers.
I said the best papers.
I suppose he will admit that the best papers are the Liberal papers. Is that what he means?
I would admit that.

The minister has been driven into many corners, but he cannot get out of this corner in that way. I want to ask the minister a fair question. I am standing here as a representative from the eastern part of Canada trying to find out if I can how this country is being governed. I do not care how it has been governed in the past; I am here to look after the present and future. If the minister wants to give the country an intimation that he is going to abolish the patronage system he can do that in no better way than by advertising in all the papers, whether Liberal or Conservative. In that way he would show the public that he meant business, that he meant what he said. Everybody knows that in the city of Halifax the ' Morning Herald,' which is an independent paper, claims to have the largest circulation of any morning paper in Canada published east of Toronto, and would it not be wise on the part of the minister when he calls for tenders in that part of the country to have an advertise-

ment put in that independent paper? Then, if the Minister of Public Works announced that he was doing away with the patronage system, the people would say: That is true, because he is advertising in other papers besides Liberal papers. I have no fault to find with him for advertising in the Liberal papers if he advertises in other papers as well. If that had been done in this case, we might have had better tenders for this work than the one we are discussing. I simply arose for the purpose of intimating to the Minister of Public Works that if he desired to inspire the people of Canada with confidence in his statement that he is going to do away with the patronage system, there is no better way of doing that than by advertising for tenders in all the influential papers in the various towns and cities, no matter what party they may support, and especially the independent papers.

I really feel very sorry for the Minister of Public Works, because last Friday he informed us that he was not satisfied with this expenditure himself, but that he could not help it because the estimates had evidently been made under his predecessor. This discussion is rather hard on the Minister of Public Works, because we know from the speech he has made in this House, that he takes the greatest care of the money of this country. Not long ago there was a resolution before this House, introduced by the hon. member for Grenville (Mr. J. D. Reid) in regard to the opening of tenders, and the Minister of Public Works told us then how carefully he would supervise the opening of tenders and what his subordinates would do. Here is one of those cases. These tenders may have been opened quite properly, but it appears to me that there is an appearance of collusion on the part of the tenderers. Here are sixteen houses built in two terraces, each house, without heating or lighting, costing roughly $5,000. Anybody who knows anything about the building of houses knows-he need not be a contractor-that $5,000 for that kind of house is simply absurd. Moreover, the cost of heating and electric lighting for these houses practically amounts to $2,000 per house. In other words, these houses are costing $7,000 apiece, and I believe we have not heard the end of them. I believe that next year we shall have a further item in the estimates, one for extras. It seems to me that estimates and tenders do not really amount to much, because there are always extras, and under the present regime what do extras mean? They mean a great addition to the cost, from the little I have seen. I want to say strongly here that the expenditure of $7,000 each for these houses, making up a total expenditure of $112,000, is a disgrace. It is something the govern-Mr. CROSBY.
ment ought to be ashamed of. I think that in future they should look better after the expenditure of the people's money. We do not want to obstruct or impede these estimates, and if we felt that the people's money were being properly expended, there would be very little opposition to them. Nearly all the opposition to the government is due to the fact that we feel that the money of the people of Canada is not being properly expended. It is time for a change in this respect, and, by Jove, if there is not, you will see that your party will be out the next time.
I would like to ask the minister what rate of pay do the men get who are going to occupy these houses?

I cannot say at the moment the exact rates of pay, but I am having a list made up, and this evening I will be able to give the rates of pay. I may say that the name ' servants' quarters ' is altogether a misnomer. The people who are occupying the buildings are teachers and instructors, with the rank of noncommissioned officers, and some of them are civilian instructors in connection with the Royal Military College. These men are getting from $1,000 to $1,600 each, possibly some of them more.

I shall have the information to-night. But before we rise at six, I want to say that all the excavation for these sixteen buildings was made in solid rock. Kingston, as we know, is a limestone city. Then all the floors in the basement were cemented. In every dwelling part, there is a bath room, and the buildings were made as near fireproof as possible All the partitions are of solid brick, as the chief architect tells me, and the walls are nine inches thick.
Are the division walls upstairs of brick as well?

Yes, the partition walls all the way up between these 16 different cottages are of brick, nine-inch walls. Then on the first floor there are many other walls similarly of brick, as the architect tells me.
There is a distinction between the partition walls of the houses and the wails between the rooms?
The partition walls between the rooms are not of brick.
