The Minister of Public Works stated the other evening that those public works for which an appropriation had been made and which had not been gone on with, would receive the first consideration of the government when it was felt they had money enough to proceed with the erection of public works.
Speaking as a general rule.
Now, there is no doubt that a great many of these public works were promised for purely political purposes.
Oh, no.

Oh, yes. The minister cannot deny that; it admits of no denial and therefore we will take it for granted. Now that the elections are over and the purpose for which these promises were made served, I do not think it would be fair to give the preference to these buildings which were promised because of a reason which was not in the public interest. It would be only fair to disregard the fact that appropriations had been made to all these towns and commence afresh, placing those places for which no appropriation had been made on exactly the same plane as those named in the Appropriation Act. In that way we would have a better distribution of public money; if we left political feeling out of consideration we would find plenty of other towns larger, more important, and producing more revenue than the ones enumerated that would deserve consideration from the minister.
I am surprised beyond measure at my hon. friend's ideas of political morality.
Do not be surprised.

My hon. friend, as an old and experienced member of the great Conservative party, intimates that in my position he would absolutely ignore the appropriations made last session, suggesting that these appropriations may have had an effect on the public mind and that we should not carry out the promises made by the Appropriation Act. If he were in my position I am sure he would not attempt to humbug the electorate in that way. I honestly believe, whether rightly or not, that every public work provided for in the estimates of last year was necessary and in the public interest, and I would be ashamed as a minister to say that no weight should be given to the fact that parliament last session made appropriations for these various works. As I have said I feel there is a solemn obligation resting on me to carry out these works for which appropriations were granted last parliament. In my constituency, and I think I can say the same thing for my friends throughout Canada in every constituency in which public buildings were promised, there was no contingency with respect to them; the public was informed, through the Appropriation Act and the estimates brought down to parliament, that these different works were regarded as reasonably necessary in the public interest and the good faith of parliament was pledged to Mr. HENDERSON.
the carrying out of these promises. Therefore I say, speaking as a general rule, that I would feel bound to continue the public works for which appropriations were made, regardless of the constituency in which they were situated. It may be that I may get further information. If my hon. friend knows of any work in his constituency that is unnecessary in the public interest, he might present his views to me. If any member thinks that a public work which has been provided for in his constituency should be dropped he has only to call my attention to the fact, and I will weigh carefully the reasons advanced.

I have listened with pleasure to the jocular remarks of the minister, whose smiling countenance showed that he was merely seeking to create a pleasing impression. I thought a mistake was made when the minister was asked to carry out an undertaking which had been promised. It is all very well for the minister to say that the political exigencies are not considered in these matters. I do not think even his own political friends will give him credit for entire sincerity in that statement. No public buildings in my riding will be left out of consideration, even although he does not adhere to the rule laid down, because there were no appropriations for any, nor has a public building ever been erected in it, so I am absolutely free to speak on this matter. The minister may think my criticism was severe, but I am satisfied that members felt last session when these appropriations were going through the House, that many of them were made simply in view of the approaching election. I believe a fair plan would be that all appropriations dropped by the minister this year should be considered as having lapsed, and when the minister takes up the matter again and money is sufficiently plentiful to go on with the construction of public works, he should begin afresh, leaving out of consideration everything that had been promised before and giving all towns and villages throughout the country an equal show.

Is it the intention to carry out a promise made by the government candidate in my county as to the erection of a post office in Hagersville? In that village a remarkable vote was cast for the government candidate, which was wholly attributable to the fact that he was able to promise a beautiful post office to be built on a beautiful site in the village of Hagersville. I am quite anxious that such a post office should be built there, and I hope the minister will carry out the promise made by the candidate in the last election. The site selected is an admirable one, nicely located in the centre of the town, which is a thriving centre, and I hope that my opponent in making that

promise, did so with the assurance of the government that they would carry it out. No doubt the minister assured him that if he were elected, that a post office would be built, and now that the county elected myself as an independent representative of the people, surely he will not for that reason go back on his promise. The labouring men there are most anxious to get work on this particular post office, as they were told they would be paid very high wages, and for that reason they voted for the government candidate.
Lest my silence might imply that any such promise was made, I rise to say that I have no recollection of it.

It seems to have been the rule for government candidates throughout the whole country to make these promises. Are we to understand that they were made without any assurance from the government that they would be carried out? But if these promises were made by the candidates in good faith and not merely to deceive the electors, the government should carry them out, or else take the stand that they repudiate them and say that their candidates had no assurance whatever on which to base them.

The hon. gentleman has not gone so far as to say that he is personally aware of any such promise having been made. He says he understands that it was. All I can say to that, so far as the government is concerned, no promise of the kind is registered in the Appropriation Act of the last parliament.
I am about in the same position as my hon. friend who has just spoken. A promise was made by my opponent that a post office would be built in the village of Kemptville.
That is in an entirely different position because an appropriation was made and the site purchased.
I did not know that. It must have been done a short time ago, and I am very glad to hear it. I suppose I can assure the people that we will have the post office.
It will not be necessary for you to give that assurance because the post office will be built any way.
And I suppose at an early date?
As early as possible.
And this year it will be in the estimates?
It is not in the estimates of this year.

As regards these public buildings, I can hardly agree with the department in the way it proceeds. I see that for the installation of electric works and heating, one firm in Ottawa last year supplied $106,949.49 worth of work on different buildings without tender.
Which firm was that?

Ahearn & Soper. Here are some of the items. On page V-20 of the Auditor General's Report, for the Dominion Archives building, $808.69; V-23 and 24, Ottawa Royal Mint, $33,887.86; V-27, Ot-Parliament Buildings, $6,103.50; V-67, Ottawa Printing Bureau, $11,917.40; V-108, $25,083.78. And other items, V-143, $10,428.20; and V-332, $3,898.20, a total of $106,949.29. Had tenders been invited for the work necessary for any one of these items, the government would have had it done much cheaper. I am quite satisfied that had tenders been called for, there would have been $25,000 in the treasury to-day saved out of that $106,947. I do not see why tenders should not be called for these works just as for the building itself. As I understand it, the system has been to invite tenders for the building. Then the heating and electric work is extra, and word is sent to this firm to go and do this work. In this way it must cost a good deal more than if tenders were called for.

I was rather surprised at the innocence of the present minister regarding the promises of public works. He is perhaps wiser in his day and generation than were some of his predecessors. In my former election, promises were made that certain works would be carried out in my constituency, but when 1 appealed to the department, I was deliberately told that it was only an election promise.
By whom were you told?
A former minister?
Yes, and I have witnesses to prove my statement.
He must have been a younger politician than I thought.
Are we to_ understand that all contracts in excess of $5,000 must be let by public tender unless you have the authority of an order in council?

As a rule, in the case of a contract which involves an expenditure of $5,000, tenders must be called for, or the facts submitted to the Governor in Council. I feel myself bound either to call for tenders or to submit the facts to the Governor in Council. But there may be cases such as the hon. member for Grenville (Mr. J. D.

t
Reid) referred to, in which a number of small items amount in the aggregate to over $5,000. But the rule of the department is to call for tenders whenever the amount exceeds $5,000. I do not know that that applies to fittings, which perhaps can hardly be called a public work.
I understood that the minister promised to bring down the orders in council in regard to contracts amounting to over $5,000 in connection with the addition to the parliament buildings.

What I told the hon. member for South Lanark (Mr. Haggart) I would bring down were the orders in council with regard to the building of the guardhouses and the fence in connection with the Mint. I then said that I understood that there was only one order in council with respect to the addition to the parliament buildings, and that was in reference to the elevators. I have made inquiry, and find that there was no order in council for any other work apart from the original contract.

The minister's statement in regard to what I said is hardly correct. Take this item of $33,887 spent on the Royal Mint. That was for the electric work on one building. In a case of that kind, I should think that tenders should be asked for, because the chief architect of the department must know that a very large amount of that work would have to be done, and various firms should be able to estimate what they would do the work for. In every case in which the cost of the heating and lighting is likely to amount to more than $5,000, I think tenders should be asked.

I may say that I have been making inquiry into this matter, and I have given directions to the chief architect that when tenders are called for, they should as far as possible include plumbing, heating, wiring and everything else. I should say, in regard to the equipment of the Mint and the Printing Bureau with motors, that the master of the Mint selected a certain class of motor for the running, of the machinery there; I think it was the West-inghouse, which is supplied by only one concern. In such a case it would be difficult to call for tenders, as the price would differ according to the quality of the machine to be supplied. There is a good deal more difficulty in that case than there would be in regard to plumbing, heating and electric wiring. At all events, the rule which my hon. friend thinks should be adopted, I also think should be adopted as far as possible, and I have already given directions to the chief architect in respect to new buildings, as far as possible, to have the specifications cover everything, so that when the contract is let we should know as nearly as possible what the work is going to cost.

The other day the minister read a long list of public works for which appropriations amounting to hundreds of thousands of dollars were asked for last year. I want to ask one or two questions in respect to that. The first is: Did the minister, at the time he asked these appropriations, intend to proceed during the year with all the works for which they were asked? If he did not intend at that time to proceed during the year with all these works, did he indicate the works with which he did intend to proceed during the year, and those he did not intend to proceed with during the year? If there were any he did not intend to proceed with during the year, why did he ask for appropriations for them last year? If the answer be that he did intend to proceed with all these works, the next question is, why did he not proceed with them? If he did not proceed, was it because of the lack of funds? If it was because of the lack of funds, did he not know then that there would be a lack of funds for all these appropriations?
My hon. friend will have to put his questions in writing, because my memory, though pretty fair, is not equal to carrying them all.
I will put them seriatim. The first is: Did you intend last year, when you asked for appropriations involving hundreds of thousands of dollars

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. gentleman will please take his seat. The hon. gentleman must address the Chair, and not any one in particular.

I will then ask you, Mr. Chairman, did the hon. minister, when he submitted all these appropriations to the House a year ago, intend at that time to implement his promises? Did he intend at that time to proceed with these works, and with all of them within the year?
I think I can answer the hon. gentleman. When those amounts were put in the estimates, it was intended to proceed with the works as rapidly as possible.
Within the year?

Yes; and proceeding with them meant acquiring sites, preparing plans and specifications, advertising for tenders, going along just as rapidly as the officials of the department could fairly proceed with the work.

That answers the first question. The hon. gentleman has answered that a year ago; when he asked for those appropriations, he honestly and sincerely intended during the year to proceed with all the works for which appropriations were asked. The next question is: Why did the hon. minister not during the year proceed

with those different public works? I could understand very well that the hon. minister could not perhaps proceed with the whole of them, but we have scores of them
I thought the hon. member wanted to ask a question.

If you will please sit down, I want to address the Chair. The hon minister having said that at that time he intended to proceed with the whole of the wcrks, I now desire to ask him why he did not proceed with any of those in that long list?
The answer is that he did proceed.

The hon. member gave us a long list of those which he asked appropriations for and did not proceed with. The hon. minister will probably admit that there is a long list of public works for which he asked appropriations, and in respect of which he has done nothing since.

My deputy tells me that he does not think there is any work in respect to which something has not been done. In respect of some, the preliminary sketches have been dropped; in respect of some, the sites have been examined, and in many cases the sites have been selected and purchased. In some, plans have been prepared and specifications have been drawn up, so that we are ready at any time to ask for tenders. But in respect to all of them, preliminary work was done in the direction of calling for tenders, and in respect of others tenders were actually called for.
When were these preliminary sketches made? Was it during the past year just previous to the general election?

The work was begun immediately after the prorogation of parliament, immediately after the appropriations were made. General instructions were given to the officers of the department to proceed with as reasonable speed as they could.	,

I think the minister has dealt very unfairly with the public, because for months many promises had been made throughout the country, and great expectations were raised among the people that these expenditures would be made, and merchants and others began to make preparations to meet the demand for carrying on these works. Now, people have a lot of material on their hands and the business of the country is gradually coming to a standstill. Now we are told that something is wrong. There is something undigested, apparently the Department of Public Works has not digested these supplies that were given to them by the last
parliament. The result is disastrous to the country. Contractors were prepared to furnish material, manufacturers of various articles had begun to prepare them, and everybody was getting ready for the large expenditure that had been promised. And now for the government to reverse their policy and break their promises is a very serious matter to this country. A little over a year ago we passed through a serious crisis, and passed through it successfully. Now another crisis is at hand in the United States, and it is essential for this country that the wheels of commerce should be kept moving in some way. I do not think there is any public work that was suggested previous to the last election in which drawings were not made, and I trust that all these works will be gone on with this year.

The Minister of Public Works has told us of the preliminary work that was done in connection with many of these projects. I would like to ask him if a promise made by a government candidate is considered one of these preliminary works.
I would like to ask the minister if a sketch was made of the Uxbridge post office in the county of Ontario, or what other preliminary steps were taken?
We purchased the site.
When was it purchased?
Previous to the election.
When will the buildings be proceeded with ?
When parliament provides the money.
I understood the minister to say that he had furnished the House with a list of the public works for which moneys were voted last year, but which are not to be proceeded with this year?
Yes, for the province of Ontario.
Why are these expenditures not being proceeded with?

I think I have stated half a dozen times the reason why they are not being proceeded with. Last December, when we came to consider these estimates, it was brought forcibly to my attention that it was desirable to cut down my estimates for the coming year to as low a figure as possible. The appropriations which were made for buildings were not sufficient to complete them, and if they had been gone on with that it would have been necessary to ask for further appropriations.
What was the object of cutting them down?

To do what every prudent man and every prudent government should do who, wish to keep the expenditure within the revenue. It became necessary for me to cut off from the estimates of the Public Works somewhere in the vicinity of eight million dollars. Now, I was not prepared to go through these estimates item after item and select those which we should proceed with and those which we should drop, so I decided that the better way was simply to postpone the construction of a certain number of public works for another year; at all events, we drew the line sharply between those works in respect of which there has been no commencement, in regard to which tenders, had not been called prior to the time we took this decision, and in that way we cut off this large amount from the estimates. Then we also cut off a number of public works in regard to which tenders had been called for, but in respect to which there did not seem to be great urgency for the present year. My hon. friend will find for the province of Ontario a list of those in respect to which tenders were called for, but the actual carrying on of which will have to stand over.

Owing to the hard times?
Mr. PUGSLEY-. Owing to the revenue being smaller than we had anticipated.
Owing to the general business depression the minister has put off many millions of expenditure that were deemed proper a year ago.
I did not say the depression; I said owing to the decline in the revenue.
The policy of the government then is still further to encourage hard times by turning a lot of labour idle on the labour market. Is that the policy of the government?
That is an argument rather than a question.

May I ask the minister why so many thousands of men have been turned idle on the labour market by the government at a time when there is business depression, when the industries of the country are in a state of depression, and why is the government still further intensifying the depression by turning those men idle on the country?
That is an argument. If my hon. friend will ask me a question of fact I will answer him.

I want to know why the government has seen fit to turn these men, these bread winners, idle at the present Mr. PUGSLEY.
time, at a time when the business interests of the country are in a state of depression? Does the minister justify that policy? Does the minister justify that expenditure?
Mr>
PUGSLEY. (That is an argument which might appeal to some, but I know there are others who take a very different view. Whether rightly or wrongly the view which the government took was that the revenue having fallen off, it was the part of prudence to curtail the expenditures and endeavour to keep them within the income. Whether that is a wise course or not, my hon. friend, as well as others, must form their own judgment. My own opinion is that we did the wise and prudent thing and that the country will approve the course we have pursued. As far as our turning people out of work is concerned, we have not done that. We simply have not gone on with public works for which we did not feel we had the revenues available at the present time. We are sorry we have not been able to give more employment on these public works though it is not our fault. We are placed in a condition which we were required to meet in a proper and prudent manner and I submit that we have met it in that way.
Was the minister not aware last June when these estimates were voted that there would be a deficit?

I was aware that the
revenues were not as buoyant as they had been, but the estimates of last session were made up before the close of the last fiscal year. I did not anticipate that the depression would continue as long as it lias.

The minister has stated that plans have been prepared for certain public buildings for which appropriations were made last year and that is proof that it is the intention of the department to proceed with these works. I would like to know whether or not the preparation of plans is conclusive proof that the government will go on with certain work?

Not at all. The best evidence of whether we will go on with certain work is the fact that parliament has made the appropriation. If, as the result of the appropriation, plans are proceeded with, my hon. friend may rely with confidence, taking the appropriation and the preparation of the plans together, that it is pretty good evidence that we intend to proceed with the work and that in the ordinary course tenders will be called and contracts made.
Is it the intention of the minister to build a post office at Port Perry, in South Ontario?

I think there is no appropriation for that.

Mr. OSLER, I am afraid I cannot very well agree with my hon. friend from Viciori i and Haliburton (Mr. Hughes) in objecting to the government exercising a little economy. They have committed themselves to such wild, reckless extravagance
That is spoiling all you said before.

No, I do not think so. I say I do not think I can blame the government for exercising economy now. They have in the past committed the country to such wild, reckless extravagance, without having looked forward to the possibility of a setback, that we are face to face not with a cutting down of the estimates for this year but, I think, that for years to come the pruning knife will have to be applied to meet the terrible outlays that the government are committed to. The government have been reckless to a degree. They have made promises in every possible direction and they have committed this country to wild expenditures. The minister is very profuse in his promises that in future contracts will be let so that the country may get the benefit of reasonable competition, but he refuses to apply his remedy when he has a chance. In connection with this museum in Ottawa a contract was let for the skeleton of the building. There is not very much more than half or two-thirds of the whole cost covered by contract.
Oh, yes.
What are the figures of the original contract and what is the building going to cost?
The contract is $950,000. and the total esimated cost is $1,250,000. That includes fittings, furniture and everything.
The public building here is what I refer to.
The original contract for the new wing of the parliament buildings was $237,000, and the additional work that was given to the contractor was $44,000.
What is the total cost?
The total cost of the new wing including the improvements to this building, elevators and the ventilation system is $447,000.

The minister is very pleasant and profuse in his mild condemnation of the way in which contracts have been let hitherto when the government let a skeleton contract and then left it open to permit inside contracts to be given bv the department without tender. The minister condemned that system and said that he hoped he would let the whole contract to one contractor. In connection with these
houses in Kingston we found the sam; thing. Four men tendered, of whom one was a builder and the others were plumbers.
There was an Ottawa firm-were they not contracors?
I do not know who they were.
The firm of Doran & Devlin are contractors of large experience who have done a large amount of work.

A contract was let for a skeleton building leaving it open to the department to let separate contracts for plumbing and heating not by public tender, but at the prices which the architect or the government gave to the original contractors. The contractor of the museum building took his contract at what the minister said was a very low price, namely, $900,000, and there is extra work amounting toi $400,000 remaining to be done. We are told that this extra work is not to be tendered for. These are sub-contracts and it is in these sub-contracts where fraud is committed and where the country is robbed. There is no man of sense in this country who would carry on that work as the gov ernment proposes to do in this case. I do not care what the minister promises for the future; I say it is his duty to commence now by showing his good faith and by having all the extra work on the museum, not included in the first contract, thrown open to public tender and competition. If the minister does that he will give us some assurance that he is trying to reform his department which needs reform badly. The minister speaks of economy this year and he says he hopes that next year he will be able to go on with many of these public works, but I tell him that the chances are that next year he will have a harder time and that he will have to reduce his appropriations still further. On account of the expose in the Cassels report the people of Canada are hoping that each department of this government shall be operated on purely business principles and that there will be no reason for accusation in future against the government or any of its employees as was the case in the Marine Department. I have very little confidence in the minister's promise of future reform unless he lets this extra work on the museum by public tender.

Last session I brought to the attention of the government the necessity for a public building in Aylmer, in my constituency. We fully expected the minister would be up there during the recess to look over the ground and we were disappointed he did not come. I find that he proposes to build a post office at Glencoe with a population of 1,200, and in Leamington, which has a population of 2,500, about the same as Aylmer, and I would like to

know why there is no appropriation for a post office in Aylmer.

I did make inquiry into the claims of the town of Aylmer and I was impressed with what my hon. friend (Mr. Marshall) said and with the other information I obtained. I regret there is no appropriation for that purpose this year. It will have to stand over with others which are equally deserving.

I regret exceedingly that the member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier) does not see eye to eye with me on the question of public expenditure under present conditions. I can tell the hon. gentleman that economy and retrenchment are two different things; and I can tell him also that extravagance in the expenditure of public money is not economy. On the assurance of the Minister of Public Works we solemnly voted a year ago large sums of money for certain buildings which were declared to be absolutely necessary in the interests of the country. It is sound policy, and it is the policy in England and in France and in every civilized land that when there is depression amongst commercial enterprises, the government which ha3 the credit should come to the relief of the people by erecting public works. That is the policy that carried the Tory party through the stormy times of 1893 and succeeding years. There was a wing of the Conservative party then which went in for lopping off the mouldering branches but there was a stronger wing which held that in times of business depression the government should go on with public works and afford employment to the people. A time of stress is on us now and if these works are necessary in the interests of the country this is the time for the government to go on with them so as to afford useful employment for those who are out of work. That is a principle which will not stand contradiction for one instant among business men. If these public works were necessary before the elections, they are doubly necessary now and it is the duty of the government to go on with them and alleviate distress and suffering.

The Minister of Pub-lis Works misunderstands my position with regard to this matter. I did not ask him to abandon all the public works he has proposed; I simply asked that they should be put on the same level as to their necessity with other public works in other communities for which no appropriation had been made. As a member of the Conservative party, I desire to say, before I resume my seat, that I do not feel myself committed to the policy laid down by the hon. member for Victoria and Haliburton (Mr. Hughes).

I wish to say, in reference to some information which was asked by my hon. friend from Simcoe (Mr. Cur-Mr. MARSHALL.
rie), that it will take some days to prepare it and when it is ready I will give it to ' Hansard.'
We will have permission to discuss it at some other opportunity.
Oh, yes.

I understood from the minister that four tenders were received in connection with the servants' quarters. Two of these were from men in the contracting business, Sullivan and Doran & Devlin, of Ottawa. The tender of McKel-vey & Birch could not be considered as a tender, as no cheque accompanied it. The tender of Elliott Bros, could hardly be considered a tender because they were not in a position to carry out the contract, not being contractors, and the specifications say that a contractor shall not assign or sublet this contract or any part of it. They were hardware merchants and plumbers and incapable of carrying out the work for which they had tendered. How much of the work represented by that $34,000 was for the heating and lighting fixtures?
I could not give the information at this moment.

That is a large proportion of the total, $112,000.	$34,000 of that
is unaccounted for in the original contract.
I think we ought to have some information as to the proportion of that amount that was tendered for.
If my hon. friend will give me a memorandum of what he wants I will submit it at some convenient time and place it in 'Hansard.'
The Minister of Militia undertook to bring down the figures in connection with the salaries of these men.

I have the information. The salaries were for instructors:	One at
$3.00 a day, one at $2.25; sergeants, one at $2.45, two at $1.35, two at $1.65, eight at $22.00 a month, one at $1.50 per day, one at $2.00 per day. Rations of course are in addition.

I have checked over these items in the Auditor General's Report. I understood that these people were the subordinate staff. Last year there were just 22 men on this list of the subordinate staff. The pay of five sergeant instructors averaged $2.03 a day. I understood the Minister of Militia to say that the pay of these men ran from about $1,000 to $1,600. One bugler gets $321 a year, one storeman gets $420 a year and one labourer gets $420 a year. Then we have twelve servants at $22 a month and two butlers at $35 a month. I must confess that that answer does not help the situation as far as the Department of Pub-

lie Works goes, because we have here absolute evidence that a good many of these people inhabiting these $7,000 houses are of the servant class at $22 a month. In the western country we consider that a man is doing fairly well if he can build a $5,000 house and it seems extraordinary that people whose salaries average from $22 to $35 a month should have built for them by the people of this country houses cost-lng $5,000 and costing as much for wiring and heating as we would require to build a whole house. I cannot believe it is anything but gross extravagance in the expenditure of public money and I think the people of the west will so regard it.

I hope my hon. friend will not think me discourteous if I do not feel called upon to reply to his observations, because I have already said all that can be said. I have explained that the basement had been excavated out of the solid rock and the fireproof character of the building.
I shall now refer to the item of barrack accommodation for stables. That means accommodation for the 25 or 30 non-commissioned officers and men of the permanent corps who look after the horses provided for the cadets. The stables have already been built and this is for the accommodation of the men who look after the horses.
This is a kind of annex to the servants' quarters.
Are the stable men to reside in this building?
Yes.
Where are the buildings located?
In the Royal Military College grounds.
How many horses has the Royal Military College attached to it for the present?
About twenty-five.
What kind of a building is this?
It is built of brick- 41 by 35 feet, two and a half storys high.
When were the horses added to the college?
They are to be taken from the horse artillery.
What are the salaries of these 22 stablemen?
The sergeants about $1.65 and the men $1.50 per day.
Do they receive their rations? Mr. PUGSLEY. Yes.
Then there has just been a detachment of artillery moved to the barracks?
Yes, with their horses, to instruct the cadets.
Will they be on the pay of the Royal College?
That is a matter for the Minister of Militia to decide.

I do not think that any opposition would be made to the erection of these buildings at Kingston if we were satisfied that they were intended for permanent barrack purposes and could be readily used at any time to accommodate from 500 to 2,000 men. But on looking over the plans I find that they have all been built with the view of the one purpose to which they are being put, and there is no reason why such expensive buildings should have been erected. I do not say that the Minister of Public Works is so much to blame because he has a lot to bear on his shoulders, but I trust that when anything of this description comes up again he will see that any building of this kind of a permanent character should be erected with a view of being utilized for general purposes of the barracks or police or quarters for the men. These are not intended for that purpose, but only for the one use, and while I would like to see the men have good quarters, I do not think the country should be charged to provide such luxurious quarters for men whose pay is so low.
Kingston Veterinary Hospital, $15,000.
Is that accommodation for the stables?
Yes, it is a hospital for the horse artillery.
Are you building a mansion of $15,000 for this purpose?
That is what it costs.
Are we to understand that there are only 25 horses to be accommodated after all this outlay, and of course that $15,000 will not finish the building?
There are about 300 horses in Kingston altogether, and this hospital is intended for those which are sick.

Is this to be an isolation
hospital?
Yes, but not necessarily so.

Has the Whitby public
item been passed?
Yes.

What was the cost of the site; who recommended its purchase, and is it not a fact that an area of ground on the opposite corner, fully as large, if not a little larger, with a splendid building on it, was purchased about the same time for less than the cost of that vacant lot?

It comprises part of lots 15 and 16. It has a frontage on Barclay street of 55 feet with a depth on Dun-das street of 150 feet, and the amount paid was $5,000. We had it examined and it was reported very suitable. It would appear from the notes I have that the site was recommended by the Whitby Board of Trade. I have here a resolution of the board of trade which recites that a suitable site is available, and no doubt this is the site.
Do they recommend $5,000 as the price for it?
They do not mention any price. It was purchased from Mr. Barclay.
Why does it not appear in his name in the Public Accounts? It appears in the name of the Society of the Sons of Scotland.
I never heard that before.

I may tell the minister that a corresponding site on the opposite corner, better located than this one, and not a vancant lot, but having a three-story brick building upon it, was sold at about the same time for about half the money that this site cost; but it had not the same motive power behind it that this had.

The minister will find the item on page V-74:
Purchase price of site-Sons of >Scotland Benevolent Society, $5,000.
I wish to endorse what the hon. member for Victoria has said. There was an adjoining property, with a brick building on it, which was sold for less than half the amount this vacant property was purchased for. The department was certainly very extravagant in the price they paid for this lot. You could purchase nearly half the sites in the whole village for that price. It certainly was a most extravagant price to pay, and met with the condemnation of all reasonable men in that vicinity.

The hon. member comes from North Ontario, and is not in a position to know what the value of this site in the town of Whitby is. It is a matter of which I know something, as it is in the county town of the county from which I CGme; and I wish to say that it is the most eligible site in the town of Whitby, that it is a corner lot on the main thoroughfare of the town, that practically every business man in Mr. PUGSLEY.
the town was consulted by myself in relation to the value of that property and its eligibility for the purpose to which it was to be devoted, and that Conservatives and Liberals alike said that if it were in their possession they would not part with it for the price which the government paid for it. I have this to say in addition, that the town council and the board of trade of the town of Whitby joined in affirming that opinion as being correct, and in declaring the site to be a proper site for the purpose, and said it was cheap at the price the government were paying for it.

I venture to say that the hon. member cannot produce one man in the town of Whitby, much less the board of trade, who will state that that was not too high a price. He cannot produce one honest man in the town of Whitby who will say that it was a proper price. We are not condemning the site, but we are condemning the exorbitant price which my friend engineered for it. He knows that the opposite lot on the same thoroughfare, with a three-story brick building on it was sold about the same time for about half the sum that the government paid for this site. My hon. friend is an adept at engineering prices. We shall have something to say later on of the Oshawa harbour deal, which was engineered by my hon. friend in connection with this same riding.

My hon. friend says that no honest man in the town of Whitby can be got to say that that was a proper price. I have only to say that perhaps the honesty of men there is not of the same quality as that of the hon. gentleman who has just spoken. They are plain, blunt, honest men in the town of Whitby, who say what they mean and mean what they say. I went to them for information as to what would be a proper price in the circumstances, and I took them at their word. I took the board of trade at its word, and the town council as well; and I had the co-operation of private individuals and public bodies in saying that the government would be warranted in paying $5,000 for the site. The hon. gentleman who has just spoken came into my riding and made himself very industrious in opposition to my candidature, and no doubt made very good use on the public platform there of the representations which ho has made here to-night, and the people expressed their estimate of his judgment and his opposition to myself by returning me with the largest majority given to any candidate in South Ontario since confederation.

I would like to ask the hon. minister by what authority the hon. member for South Ontario was parading around the constituency looking for lots for post offices and other public buildings for the department? It is only in accord-

ance with the policy generally pursued by hon. gentlemen opposite, who took every opportunity to promise public buildings to the constituencies in order to secure a majority in this House; and it ill becomes the hon. member from South Ontario to show that assiduity in regard to corner lots in Whitby in order to put himself right with the electors of South Ontario. I would say, for the information of the Minister of Public Works, that the name of the gentleman from whom this lot was purchased does net appear in the Public Accounts at all. It is stated there that it was purchased from the Sons of Scotland. Why was not the name of the man from whom it was really purchased placed there? The reason was that he was an active political supporter of the hon. member for South Ontario, who busies himself with the voters' lists. In view of this fact, we can see why the government paid such an outrageous price for this vacant lot.

The hon. member for South Ontario has referred to the honour of the people of Whitby. I again make the statement that I spoke to a great many of the prominent men in Whitby, and while they were delighted to get a post office, they one and all laughed at the price, and said that it was the result of a deal with my hon. friend from South Ontario, similar to the deal that had been made with him with regard to the Oshawa harbour, when the government were induced, by misrepresentations-
Order.
Absolutely in order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The point of order having been raised, perhaps I should rule of .it. I do not understand the hon. member to be charging dishonour to any hon. member of the House, and in that case I do not rule him out of order.
The hon. gentleman who now misrepresents South Ontario

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: That I think is not in order.

The hon. gentleman who now represents South Ontario in this House induced this government to purchase the Oshawa harbour, and the charge was made upon every platform in the riding, and was not successfully contradicted, that he had done it by misrepresenting the tolls of the harbour which he controlled, and thereby induced them to pay a large price for it. As soon as he unloaded, instead of bringing his coal in through the harbour, he brought it in by rail to the town, and dumped the harbour on the government. That is the charge that is made by the electors of Oshawa, and throughout that riding. That is the charge, and the hon. member came up
and went through the town of Whitby

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I think the
hon. gentleman is wandering away from the subject, which is the Whitby public building.

I am speaking of that building. The hon. member came up to the town of Whitby 'and passed around from person to person, and everybody was naturally delighted to get a post office. But the board of trade have not stated that they endorsed the price paid for the site, the town council have not stated that they endorsed the price, nor has any public man in the town of Whitby. All of them look on it as a rake-off from start to finish.

I would ask the Minister of Public Works who it was that constituted the member for South Ontario (Mr. Fowke) a commissioner to purchase a lot for this government in the town of Whitby. He was not then a member of this House, he was not representing the county; the county was represented by an enirely different individual. How came it that the present member for South Ontario went through that county picking out lots for this government? This post office was not the only one the member for South Ontario promised to the electors of that county, and did this government appoint him as a commissioner to make those promises? Why should he take it upon himself to buy a lot in the town of Whitby for this government, if this government had not appointed him for that purpose?

My hon. friend from South Ontario, I presume, as a public man and as a candidate, had a right to do what he did. When it was contemplated by the government to purchase a lot in the town of Whitby for a public building, he had a perfect right to inform himself with regard to the value of the different sites which were spoken of, he had a perfect right, for the protection of his own interest as a candidate of the Liberal party, to inform himself as to whether the price for this lot was fair and reasonable, and I commend my hon. friend for having taken the trouble to ascertain if the price was fair and reasonable. It is all very well for hon. gentlemen opposite to deal with rumours; it is all very well for people who are dissatisfied because they did not succeed in selling their property, to disparage the property that was sold. But we have the word of the hon. member for South Ontario, whose judgment, I for one am prepared to place great reliance upon; more than that, we have the report of our own inspector, a man of large experience. He went there, as I am informed, and examined the various sites, questioned people who had lots to sell as to what they would take for their property, and after carefully considering the relative values of the different sites, he recommended that this property should be purchased.

Would the minister kindly give the price recommended by the other inspector, and who was the inspector?
_ Mr. PUGSLEY. My deputy informs me it was Mr. C. H. Hunter, a man of large experience in these matters. In the department rwe always adopt the course of requiring the most careful examination to be made into all the properties available. We asked our agent to find out at what prices properties had been recently changing hands for two or three years back, to get the assessed values of the properties, to furnish all the particulars which would enable the chief architect and the minister to form a correct judgment as to the propriety of purchasing a property which is recommended to the department.
Do I understand the minister to say that he sent two inspectors there to value the property?
An inspector, Mr. C. H. Hunter.

I think this is a serious matter that the minister has brought up. He says he upholds the member for South Ontario, that he had a perfect right to pick out this lot. The member for South Ontario states that he was the man who selected the lot. As I understand, it was he who interviewed the different parties; he was, so to speak, the whole push in connection with the selection of this particular site. The minister lays down the princinle that it is proper to place in the hands of a candidate for parliament the power to select lots for post offices. If that is the case, we should know it. That seems to have been the policy followed by the government throughout the country. They authorize their candidates to give promises of post offices wherever they like, and the member for South Ontario seems to have been favoured in that respect also. The principle is entirely wrong. If the member for South Ontario had any authority frcm this govern-men we should know what that authority is.
Has the minister the report of the inspector on that site?
I have not.
Nobody in Whitby condemned the site, the only thing they condemned was the rake-off in the extra price that was paid for this lot over and above the fair market value.
I would like to know from the minister who was the owner of the property when the transfer was made to the government.

I may say to my hon. friend that this item passed some days ago, and as I did not suppose it would come up Mr. PUGSLEY.
again to-night I did not bring with me the papers in connection with the site. But I could get the papers and bring them down for the information of my hon. friend. The real owner, I presume, would be the Sons of Scotland. Possibly Mr. Barkley had a mortgage, but the Department of Justice would attend to the title, that would not come under my supervision. When we decide to purchase a property we transfer the papers to the Department of Justice, and if the title is found good, the cheque is made out to the agent of the Minister of Justice to pay the owner. In this case I presume the Sons of Scotland were the owners of the property.
Who was the agent of the Minister of Justice ?
I do not know.
Would the member for North Ontario tell us who was the owner of this lot?

My information was that it was a political supporter of the member for South Ontario, Mr. L. T. Barkley. Would the minister kindly say whether the member for South Ontario had any authority from the department, either to recommend or to inspect the various lots in the town of Whitby?

By looking up the papers I could ascertain if there was any communication in reference to the matter, but I have not the papers with me to-night. But so far as the action of the hon. member for South Ontario is concerned in this matter, I thoroughly approve of it. I approve of the hon. gentleman having taken an interest in securing a public building for the town of Whitby. I think it would be entirely within his right as a public man seeking the suffrages of the people, to interest himself to the extent of seeing that a suitable location was secured for a public building. I think he was entirely within his right in ascertaining the value of the various properties, and to satisfy himself that the price asked for the lot in question was a fair and reasonable price, so that the government might not be criticised, and that he himself as a supporter of the government might not be criticised, in respect to the purchase.
Would the Minister of Public Works give us the name of the agent of the government to whom this cheque was made payable?
I will be very glad to do it, but I cannot do it to-night.

I do not think this committee should agree with the principle laid down by the Minister of Public Works. That principle is a most vicious one, a most reprehensible one and one which is capable

of the greatest possible abuse. If candidates for the government can be empowered by the different departments to go around towns and municipalities and represent themselves as the accredited agents of the government it is capable of the greatest possible abuse. I am surprised to hear the minister lay down a doctrine of that kind because it is demoralizing to the whole community. A practice similar to that was carried on in the town of Uxbridge in South Ontario. The day after the writ^were issued we had an accredited agent of the department around with the friends of Mr. Grant, my opponent in the election, taking options on all the corner lots in the town, holding out inducements and raising the expectations of the electors that if my opponent were elected an expensive post office would be erected in the town. Now we have the minister allowing this ontion to lapse and doing nothing although there was $8,000 in last year's estimates for this work. The principle enunciated by the minister is a most vicious one and one worthy of the most severe condemnation.
Is my hon. friend old enough in politics to let us know what policy his party followed previous to 1896?
I would like the minister to read the communication from the Board of Trade.

This is the resolution:
Whereas a suitable site satisfactory to the whole community is at present available. The Whitby office is a distributing centre for a considerable and important district. Whitby is the county town of one of the richest counties in _ the province; and as the various court sittings and the sessions of the county council are held here the offices of the general government should be in keeping with the other public buildings.
If a government building were, erected the customs and postal services could be combined under one roof, instead of being carried on as now in two buildings poorly equipped and a considerable distance apart.
The cost of constructing such a building would not exceed the capitalized rental of the present buildings.
The expenditure in the present case could be amply justified by the existing and pressing need as being in the public interest.
Be it therefore resolved- that the attention of the Dominion government be called to this matter in the hope that steps may at once be taken to secure the erection of a new customs and post office, suitable to the present and advancing needs of the town of Whitby and that a copy of this resolution be forwarded to the Premier, the Postmaster General and the Minister of Public Works.

That is not the resolution that the minister referred to. We want the resolution endorsing this site.
49i
This is the resolution.
There is no site referred to there.
It says ' Whereas a suitable site satisfactory to the whole community is available.'
That meant any site.
I told my hon. friend that this resolution did not name the site, but I presumed that it referred to this site.

The minister gave the committee to understand that a resolution had been passed by the board of trade endorsing the site selected by the hon. member for South Ontario. The minister inferentially lets the committee believe that they have endorsed the site and the price. They do not say so and the member for South Ontario finds himself in rather an unfortunate position.
I regret that my hon. friend's memory should be so fickle.
My memory is all right and ' Hansard ' will bear me out.

My hon. friend will remember that I stated distinctly that while the resolution did not mention the particular site selected, it referred to the fact that there was a suitable site then available and I presume that referred to the site which was actually purchased.
Does the minister say that Whitby is a customs port?
The application was for a customs house and post office as well. I am unable to state whether it is or not.
What is the date of that resolution?
It is dated March 6. 1907.
By whom was it signed?
John Waugh, secretary.
At what date was the purchase made?
There was an order in council passed on the 25th October, 1907, for the purchase and I presume the purchase would follow shortly after that.
How much is the new building in Whitby to cost?
I am afraid I have not that information to-night. This item passed three or four days ago and I did not bring the papers back.

I understand that $43,000 has been appropriated. It will cost about

$50,000. The resolution says that the interest capitalized is not going to amount to more than the present rental. What rental is being paid?
At that time it was $330.

Interest on $50,000 would be
about $2,000.	.
I think the board of trade were rather within the mark.

They were talking through their hats when they made that statement in the resolution.
Public Works-Cha rgeable to Income-* Dauphin Public Building, $24,000.

I would like to ask the minister whether or not he has been able to carry out all the pledges that were made in the province of Manitoba? How many public works promised last session and voted have been dropped? If. he will give us that list we will then be in a better position to discuss the items as they come up.

I take it that my hon. friend is not very busy at the present moment and if he will take the Appropriation Act of last year, then take these estimates and subtract one from the other he will see exactly.

I admit that I have not been very busy and that I have been sitting here listening to the discussion of these items. The minister took the trouble to make a list for Ontario and I am not asking anything more than he did in the case of Ontario.
I will do it a little later; I cannot do it at this moment.
I think the minister should give us that information before we begin to deal with these estimates.

I would like to draw the attention of the Minister of Public Works to the fact that there was an appropriation last year for a post office at Elmwood, Man. Previous to the election the county was visited by my opponent, Mr. Jackson, and he called a meeting of the Liberals of that town to select a site. I understand that a site was selected and I was told by the minister that the site was bought on the 6th October. The promise was given by my opponent, Mr. Jackson, that the building of a post office would be proceeded with immediately and I would like to ask the minister if it is his intention to implement that pledge? I presume that when the vote was made it was the intention of the government to proceed with the work. I also presume that my opponent, Mr. Jackson, had full authority to make the promise he made to the electors of Elmwood that a post office Mr. OSLER.
costing $40,000 would be proceeded with immediately. What has caused the government to change its policy in this regard, because I see that the vote for the Elmwood post office is dropped out of the estimates this year?

I suppose I will have to explain it to my hon. friend again if he will not take the trouble to read ' Hansard.' The appropriation for the public building^at Elmwood last year was put in the estimates upon the earnest solicitation of the late member, Mr. Jackson, and it having been voted by parliament Mr. Jackson would have perfect authority for informing the people that the government had decided to erect that building. The fact that a site had been purchased would I presume justify him in stating that it was the intention of the government to proceed with the building without delay. That was the intention of the government when the appropriation was made, but for the reason that the revenues have declined and that we feel it prudent in the public interest to keep our expenditure within our revenue there is no vote for the Elmwood ' post office this year. We have treated Elmwood no differently from scores of other places throughout the Dominion. We do not treat it differently because it has, shall I say the bad fortune or the good fortune, to have my hon. friend (Mr. Bradbury) as its representative. My hon. friend can rely that having purchased the site it simply means a postponement of the building for a reasonable time.

I would point out to the Minister of Public Works that when these very items were being voted for public buildings last year the Minister of Finance had announced in his Budget Speech that he anticipated a falling off of $6,000,000 in the revenue, and in face of that announcement the government voted these appropriations.

We are providing this year for dredging rivers and harbours and for the erection of a large number of public buildings, and in view of the shrinkage in revenue being double what the hon. gentleman says was anticipated, I think we are doing very well that we have kept over one-half of our estimates for public works in the appropriations for this year.

I quite understand that the Minister of Public Works has to answer the same questions over and over again, but if there were any consistency in the position assumed by him it would be less difficult for him to explain it. If we could discern a thread of logic running through his argument we would not be so insistent in our demand for information. As we pointed out last Friday evening, the Minister of Public Works stated in July last.

in reply to the hon. member for Peel, that there absolutely need be no concern about the erection of these public works, and that there was no cause for alarm that any accident would interfere with their being proceeded with. The logical result of this statement was that these buildings for which appropriations were taken would be erected. On looking into the matter I find that the very month that the minister made that assertion to the House was the month in which the revenue of the country fell to the largest extent below the revenue for the corresponding period in the previous year. I find that for the four months of the fiscal year, commencing on the 1st April and ending with the month in which the minister made that statement, the revenue of the country fell off by some $6,789,589.35, or at the rate of $1,697,397.34 per month. Now, from the end of July to the end of the current^ year, the falling off in the revenue diminished, so that commencing with the 1st of August, 1908, and ending with the very month when the minister decided on a retrenchment of $8,000,000 the revenue declined at one-half the rate of the previous period, or $933,577 per month.
Order.

The hon. gentleman has called me to order, but I really think I am closer to the point than many hon. members on this side of the House have been, or than the minister himself has been throughout this debate.
That has been discussed so often.
This has never been discussed before.
This is the fifth or sixth time we have heard your speech.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: As the point has been raised, I think that in discussing Supply the opposition is entitled to a great deal of freedom and I have not felt that the remarks of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Meighen) are out of order on the vote for public buildings in Manitoba.

I have endeavoured to show that the, reasons given by the minister for the policy entered on by the government in December last are not logical, and particularly so in the light of the fact that in July last, when these estimates were voted, not only was July the month of the largest decrease in our revenue over the corresponding period of the previous year, but the fact stands out in strong contrast that the very month in which the ministry arrived at the decision that there must be retrenchment, namely, two months after the election, was the only month in the year 1908 in which the revenue exceeded that of the corresponding month for
the preceding year. The revenue for December, 1908, was $7,183,355.94. The revenue for 1907 was $7,093,530.87, so that there was an actual increase in the revenue for December, 1908, of some $933,000, or about $3,000 a day over the corresnonding month of the year before. Thus the logic of the minister amounts to this, that when the revenue is falling off at the greatest rate he has cause to assure this country that there is no cause for concern, that he will be able to erect all the structures that he dangles before the electors and just as soon as the revenue resumes its equilibrium and reaches or surpasses the revenue of the year before, the minister in his logic arrives at the conclusion that he must retrench. It will be difficult for the minister to convince the House that that is the real position or the real reason that animated him. The Minister of Finance apparently was the monitor. It was at his suggestion that this decision was reached in December, 1908. I am glad to see him at the right hand of the Minister of Public Works to-night. We are justified in concluding that if the Minister of Finance was the monitor in December, 1908, he was the monitor also in July, 1908. Some three months before that the Minister of Finance, speaking on the 17th of March, assured the House that he anticipated the revenues would fall off by some six and a-half millions and probably by more than that amount. By the time July had arrived the revenue had fallen off by more than that amount, so that if the Minister of Finance were the monitor in December and also in July he surely must have told his colleague that he was only deceiving the public by saying it was possible to go on with this work because the revenue had already decreased by over $6,500,000. On the whole there is every ground to question the reason which the minister has given to-night and other nights, every reason to look back and to say that it is to meet the exigencies of the election that these two months elapsed and that the minister just at the time he had the only reason he ever had to go on with these works, on the contrary decided that he would abandon them for this year at least. I cannot accept the reason of the minister at all and I do not think the country can. I asked last Friday for a return relating to advertisements.
I brought that down this evening.
From whom was the Elmwood site purchased?
Would my hon. friend allow me to give him that to-morrow?
How much has been expended for Dauphin public building?
When the estimate was made up $8,000 had been paid on the contract over and above the site.
I insist on the minister giving me a list of the works abandoned in Manitoba just as he gave a list to the members from Ontario. I think we are entitled to it.

I trust my hon. friend will not be unreasonable. He could not expect me, while going through with these items, to sit down and do what my hon. friend would be able to do, that is to take the account of last year and these estimates and subtract one from the other.
I presume, the minister has that information?
No, I have not it with me.
Would the minister give the particulars of this contract?
The contract price is $20,330, including the building, but not the heating, wiring, fittings or fixtures.
What did the site cost?

What will the building cost when completed?
_ Mr. PUGSLEY. About $32,000. The lot is 75 x 132 feet on Burrows avenue.
Is it a corner lot?

I do not think so.
Dominion Public Buildings, renewals, improvements, repairs, &c., $10,000.
Will that item include the furnishing of the Selkirk post office?
We expect the furnishing to be finished before March 31 and paid out of the appropriation for the present fiscal year.
I would like an explanation about the public building at Emerson.

It is being built on a lot
60 by 140 feet, required for post office and customs purposes. The site cost $1,000. Estimated total cost of building $34,000, including furnishing, fittings and fixtures.
Will this complete the building?

Yes.
Winnipeg Customs Warehouse, $175,000.

In connection with the expenditure, I find in the Auditor General's Report, V-77, an item, 'purchase price of additional land for 'site. J. H. Kern.' The other day a question was asked regarding the terminals. Kern, it appears, was the man from whom these terminals were purchased. He was planted in there at a very convenient time between the former owner and the government, and Mr. PUGSLEY.
the report was that he got a rake-off of $122,000. This man Kern is a very agile person. We find that he is transplanted here between the owner and the former owner of the land in the purchase of the site of this warehouse. Is this the same Kern mentioned in the other case from whom the land was purchased for the terminals ?
Is that for the new examining warehouse?
Yes, he is a hotelkeeper at Moosejaw.
This land was bought before I became minister. My impression is it was purchased from Mackenzie and Mann.
There were two portions. This was for an addition to the site. The original portion was bought from Mackenzie and Mann.
There may have been a small piece bought from Kern.

$35,000 paid to Kern is a pretty considerable item. There will be a chance for a benefit to him here in addition to the benefit he got from the other transaction. When the government have such reliable inspectors and agents, it will be proper to call this matter to the attention of the inspector. I may tell the minister, for his information, that this Mr. Kern is not there for his sole benefit. The people of Winnipeg know, or soon will know that either the government or some friend of the government, or some mutual friend of the government and Mr. Kern succeeded in putting him in there as a stool pigeon for a certain purpose, and perhaps not the most laudable purpose.
Does the hon. gentleman say that the price paid was too high?
I think that $35,000 for a little piece of land pn a back street was a little too high.
How much land was there?
I do not know. We are here for the purpose of ascertaining that.
The information I have is that the land was purchased from Mackenzie and Mann for $88,125.
How much was bought from the other man?
I have no memo of land bought from any one else.
We would like this cleared up because it was the subject of Ivery common conversation among the business men of Winnipeg.

The hon. gentleman is speaking of a different building altogether. There was some land purchased from Mr. Kern for an immigration building which is a different item. This is for a customs warehouse.
Winnipeg Post Office Building-Fitting up ground and first floors, $25,000.
This is an old building. We had built a new post office.

That brings to my mind the question of some litigation as regards the ownership of the old building. Now that you have vacated it as a post office, I have seen articles in the press stating it is going to revert back to the original owners.
I have heard nothing about that. The building is still to be occupied as a public building for Customs purposes and Inland Revenue and Assistant Receiver General.
Would it be convenient to have that used as a custom house when the examining warehouse and the other buildings are so far from it?
The examining warehouse adjoins the old post office building.
It must be at least a quarter of a mile from the present examin ing warehouse. Is it the intention to move all the customs business to that locality?

The Customs Department have asked for this accommodation, and we are giving it to them. I do not know whether they intend to move the entire business there or not. I understand that the Department of the Interior will use the old customs house for' a land office.

If the hon. minister looks up the records of his department, I think he will find that there are communications in reference to the matter referred to by the hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Staples). I remember hearing that matter discussed in the House in the time of the hon. gentleman's predecessor. I think a gentleman named Ballantyne owned the site in question, and donated it on the condition that it should be retained by the government as a post office site. When the matter was brought before the hon. minister's predecessor, he admitted that there were communications to that effect, and promised to bring them down at an early day, but failed to do so.
I will have the matter looked up, if the hon. member will call my attention to it at some later day.
I do not see any provision in the estimates this year for the post office north of the track in Winnipeg. Is that completed?	 i
It will be completed before the end of the present fiscal year.

What did that building
cost?
I have not the papers at present, and cannot say.

Can the minister inform the House who are the contractors for the fixtures for the north-end post office and the Selkirk post office, or was a contract let? My information leads me to believe that a contract was let for the fixtures of those two post offices, and that a man very high in the service of the post office is a large shareholder in the company furnishing those buildings. I am told in Selkirk that that accounts largely for the delay in opening the Selkirk post office. Although the building has been completed for at least six months, I do not think) it is furnished yet.

As I am not asking tonight for a vote for either of these buildings, I have not the papers with me regarding them. If my hon. friend will put the question in the House, I will with pleasure get the information in regard to both of them.

I would like the minister to explain why the appropriations for Manitoba are cut down to such a very large extent this year, while those for other provinces are not cut down nearly so much. The appropriations for Alberta, Saskatchewan and Northwest Territories are cut down by $305,000, while those for Manitoba alone are cut down $346,876.

My hon. lriend, on reflection, will see that, adopting the rule which I said we had adopted with regard to postponing public buildings, there might be an undue proportion cut off from one province as compared with another. For instance, take my own province of New Brunswick ; the appropriations for public buildings have been cut down from $134,100 last year to $21,500 this year. Those for Nova Scotia have been cut down from $282,300 to $132,600. The appropriations for Quebec have been cut down from $1,571,249 last year to $525,600 this year, only one-third of what they were. The appropriations for Ontario have been cut down from $1,453,175 to $605,367, a reduction of more than fifty per cent. So that" there is no rule in regard to the matter.

There may not be the same inducement this year that there was two or three years ago, when it was said that a post office valued at nearly half a million was built as an annex to a large printing establishment on Portage avenue owned by an ex-minister.

The figures given by the minister in his answer should be taken in conjunction with the figures of the amount unspent in each province. If that is done, they show a marked disparity against the province of Manitoba.
Public Buildings-Saskatchewan, Alberta and Northwest Territories, $352,000.

I wish to bring to the attention of the minister a very urgent case in my constituency. A very small amount was asked for in the estimates of last year to protect the town of Macleod. I have already spoken to the minister personally on the subject, and I would like to impress upon him the importance of that work.
Is that the protection work?
Yes, the protection of the banks of the streams.

I would ask the hon. gentleman to leave that until we come to the harbours and rivers. We are now on puijiic works.
Lethbridge-Custom House and Dominion Lands Office, $1,000.

In the estimates of last year there was $6,000 for this work. I would like to ask the hon. gentleman why the work did not proceed. I happen to know that there was every reason for it to be gone on with, because the Dominion Lands office, which occupies part of that building, is sorely in need of further office room. The court house in the upper part of that building has been vacant for a year waiting these improvements.
I cannot give the hon. gentleman the reason why it has not been proceeded with more rapidly; but $2,000 has been expended upon it, or will be before the close of the fiscal year.
I do not think there has been any money expended at all. Up to the 10th of December, when I left, not a dollar had been spent.
We expect to expend $2,000 before the 31st of next month, and we are here asking for a revote.
Does the minister intend that this work will be proceeded with in the spring?
Yes.

I would like some assurance, because, as I say, better facilities are absolutely required. In the Dominion Lands office there is only a space in front of the counter about the size of the table Mr. A. HAGGART.
before us. People have to stand out in the street.
The engineers have instructions to push these improvements in the spring.

I wish to bring another matter to the attention of the minister, although it is not in the estimates, and that is the necessity of a post office building in Lethbridge. I want to enunciate here the position I take in connection with the expenditure of public money. I do not believe that any town is ever going to make headway merely through the expenditure of public money therein. I do not think it means any advancement to a town to have government moneys spent there just for the purpose of getting a large building, and while I am in this House I do not mean ever to advance any such argument. I do not subscribe to the policy that is pursued in this country in reference to the erection of public buildings. Go through the country from one end to the other and you find post offices costing many thousands of dollars in small places where there is no necessity for such costly buildings, due, I suppose we may frankly admit, to political pressure. I hope that I shall not be found advocating expenditures with the hon. gentleman on any such ground. Lethbridge has to-day a population, I have been told, of 7,500, but I will call it 7,000. I have a letter from the Post Office Department which says in reference to a post office:
Practically the only way the difficulty can he overcome is by the erection of a public building.
The post office there is in a rented building and the post office authorities know that the facilities are not at all adequate. As I am interested in the question, I have been looking up statistics, and I find that the Postmaster General last March stated that there were ten post offices built since 1904, and 31 post offices under construction. I made a list of some of these post offices, which I submit to the committee:
